findings.claim: The new teaching sentence says the three-argument groupingBy's 'middle argument is a constructor reference'. The Java SE 25 parameter is mapFactory, 'a supplier providing a new empty Map'; a constructor reference such as TreeMap::new is one way to supply it, not a requirement. A local JDK 17.0.12 run with groupingBy(Ticket::level, () -> new TreeMap<>(Comparator.reverseOrder()), counting()) compiles and prints {low=2, high=2}. The page's own example and answer are unaffected. The coverage plan section 2 repeats the wording ('whose middle argument is a map-factory constructor reference').

evidence.section: groupingBy(Function, Supplier, Collector): parameter 'mapFactory - a supplier providing a new empty Map into which the results will be inserted'

findings.recommendation: Reword to 'its middle argument is a map factory, a supplier usually written as a constructor reference such as TreeMap::new, that chooses which kind of map holds the groups' (and the same in the generated artifact.md and coverage plan section 2).

findings.claim: Option B's explanation (and its data-static-alt copy) ends 'every check scans the whole line'. ArrayDeque.contains is documented as linear time, which is the correct reason the option fails, but contains stops at the first match; it scans the whole deque only when the id is absent or last. 'Every check scans the whole line' overstates a linear-time cost as a full scan.

evidence.section: Class description: 'Most ArrayDeque operations run in amortized constant time. Exceptions include remove, removeFirstOccurrence, removeLastOccurrence, contains, iterator.remove(), and the bulk operations, all of which run in linear time.'

findings.recommendation: Say 'each check may scan the whole line, so its cost grows with the number of waiting tickets' (or 'scans the line until it finds the id'). Update the static alternative and artifact.md to match.
